stem: A bag contains 4 white balls and 6 black balls. Two balls are drawn one after another without replacement. Given that the first ball drawn is white, what is the probability that the second ball drawn is also white?

per_option_rationale.rationale: After one white ball is removed, 3 white balls remain out of 9 total. P = 3/9 = 1/3.
Using P(white) from the original 10 balls: 4/10 = 2/5, ignoring that one white ball has already been drawn and treating draws as independent.
Correctly reducing the total to 9 but forgetting to reduce the white count, using 4/9 instead of 3/9.
Reducing the white count to 3 but keeping the total at 10: 3/10, not accounting for the removal in the denominator.

explanation: Without replacement, removing one white ball changes the composition. After the first (white) draw: whites left = 3, total balls left = 9. P(2nd white | 1st white) = 3/9 = 1/3.

explanation_sections.punchline: Without replacement, every draw changes both the numerator and denominator of the next probability.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the model: conditional probability via updated sample space. Initial: 4 white, 6 black, 10 total. After one white drawn: 3 white, 9 total. P = 3/9 = 1/3.
explanation_sections.lesson: In without-replacement draws, always track both the remaining favourable count and the remaining total.
explanation_sections.timing: 60 seconds. Update both counts, divide. The classic trap is keeping either the numerator (4/9) or the denominator (3/10) unchanged.
